name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Tuesday 15 May 1990 (English cryptic)

clue.text: Letter making silly sap very annoyed

indicators.note: silly suggests things put in a foolish, disordered state, so the next word's letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
irate means very angry

explanation.surface: A letter written in such a temper that it makes some fool furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' looks like correspondence, but it means a letter of the alphabet: an aspirate is the breathy H sound, or the letter H itself.
explanation.definitionFit: In phonetics an aspirate is a breathed consonant, and the term is used for the letter H that represents it.

clue.text: A Length of timber on a sea-going vessel

blocks.note: taken as written
a board is a long flat piece of sawn wood

explanation.surface: A plank lying on the deck of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Aboard means on or onto a ship, so it fits a phrase about being on a vessel.

clue.text: Not all people, as everyone knows, are agreeable

definitions.note: a verb phrase; the answer is the verb to please

indicators.note: not all says only part of the following words is used

blocks.note: the letters running across the end of the first word, the second, and the start of the third
surface padding completing the phrase as everyone knows

explanation.surface: A general truth: not everybody is nice, as we all know.
explanation.definitionFit: To please is to be agreeable to someone, giving them satisfaction or pleasure.

clue.text: Soldiers grow weary, so get leave

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
to tire is to become weary

explanation.surface: The troops are exhausted, so they are granted time off.
explanation.definitionFit: To retire is to withdraw from a place or from work, as one does when given leave to go.

clue.text: Call in expert — may be finished

blocks.note: to term something is to call it by a name
taken as written
able means skilled or expert

explanation.surface: Bring in a specialist, as the job might then be completed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call in' looks like a phrasal verb, but the words split: one is a verb for naming, the other stays as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Something terminable is capable of being ended, such as a contract that can be brought to a close.

clue.text: Getting off before the terminus, tread on people's toes

indicators.note: before says the first part is placed ahead of the second in the answer

blocks.note: getting off a vehicle means getting off it: the word off itself
a terminus is the end of the line

explanation.surface: A bus passenger who pushes past everyone to get out a stop early.
explanation.definitionFit: To tread on people's toes is an idiom for upsetting them, which is what giving offence does.

clue.text: Tureen of mash which serves a number

indicators.note: to mash is to crush into a pulp, so the letters before it are broken up and reformed

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: A big bowl of mashed potato that feeds quite a few diners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serves a number' sounds like portions for several people; the answer is a number itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Fourteen is a specific whole number, twice seven, so it is an example of a number.

clue.text: The Spanish accommodating the Red King at one time

indicators.note: accommodating means giving room to, so one part is housed inside the other

blocks.note: el is the Spanish word for the
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Spain playing host to a communist ruler of the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red King' reads as one figure, perhaps from Alice; the colour stays as it is and only 'King at one time' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethelred was the name of Anglo-Saxon kings, most famously Ethelred the Unready, so a monarch of old.

clue.text: Sidney turned the lock, causing much trouble

indicators.note: turned means facing the opposite way, so the short form of the name is read backwards

blocks.note: Sid is the usual short form of Sidney
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: A man named Sidney turned a key and caused a great deal of bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' suggests a door; here it is a lock of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Distress is acute suffering or hardship, a great deal of trouble.

clue.text: A proposal to have nothing green by the river

indicators.note: by means next to, so the last part sits alongside what comes before it

blocks.note: nothing is zero, the letter O
vert is green in heraldry
the Ure is a Yorkshire river, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A suggestion to leave the riverbank bare of any greenery.
explanation.walkthrough: Vert is the heraldic word for green, from the French.
explanation.definitionFit: An overture is an opening offer or approach made to start negotiations, so a proposal.

clue.text: Charges for some plants

blocks.note: first meaning: dashes headlong at, as a charging animal does
second meaning: tall marsh plants with hollow stems

explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' reads as fees; it is the verb for running at something.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for hurtling forward and the plural name of grasslike waterside plants.

clue.text: Check trainers' organisation

indicators.note: an organisation is an arrangement, so the preceding letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: the letters as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: An instruction to inspect the body that governs racehorse trainers.
explanation.definitionFit: To check something is to hold it back or curb it, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Flatter Socialist leader with a report, right?

indicators.note: a leader is the one at the front, so only the opening letter of the word before it is used

blocks.note: its leading letter
a tale is an account or report of events
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A political question: does the socialist leader's report butter up the right wing?
explanation.walkthrough: The scan's OCR prints 'Ratter'; the wordplay and grid need 'Flatter', meaning more flat, as beer goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer or bread that is staler has lost its freshness and fizz, so it is flatter.

clue.text: The manager is against a fellow fishing

blocks.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
a troller fishes by trailing a baited line behind a boat

explanation.surface: The boss disapproves of a colleague going off fishing.
explanation.definitionFit: A controller is someone who directs or manages an organisation or department.

clue.text: They operate constantly under pressure

blocks.note: surface reading: overworked staff who are always stressed
setter's reading: instruments whose working depends on atmospheric pressure

explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like workers in a stressful job; it literally describes weather instruments that respond to air pressure at all times.
explanation.definitionFit: These instruments measure atmospheric pressure, so they are always working under it, literally.

clue.text: Non-professional persons, mature as can be

indicators.note: can be suggests what the preceding letters are able to become when arranged differently

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: Unpaid enthusiasts who are as grown-up as anyone could be.
explanation.definitionFit: Amateurs take part in an activity for pleasure rather than pay, so they are not professionals.

clue.text: The beast has to run after a worker with a key

indicators.note: after places the running part behind the others in the answer

blocks.note: a worker ant, the crossword's standard worker
E is a musical key
to lope is to run with long easy strides

explanation.surface: An animal must chase an employee who is carrying a key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' suggests a door; here it is a musical key named by a letter from A to G.
explanation.definitionFit: An antelope is a swift, horned grazing animal of Africa and Asia, so a beast.

clue.text: Make notes about a point for speech

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase; the answer is used adjectivally, as in a speaking part

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the musical verb wraps around the other part

blocks.note: to sing is to produce musical notes
a peak is a pointed top

explanation.surface: Jot down something on one topic so you can deliver a talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make notes' suggests writing; it means producing musical notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking describes something used for talking, as in a speaking tube or a speaking role.

clue.text: Many turned up in a previous work

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so the three short words after it are read backwards

blocks.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a crossword stand-in for many
taken as written, then read backwards
late means previous, as in the late chairman

explanation.surface: Lots of people showed up in an earlier piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' looks like a phrase for arrived, but 'turned' works on the next three words together. 'Work' is a verb here: to work clay is to handle it skilfully.
explanation.definitionFit: To manipulate something is to handle or shape it with skill, which is one sense of working it.

clue.text: Drink not paid for — there could well be soda in it

definitions.text: there could well be soda in it

blocks.note: to sip is to drink a little
Hon. is short for honorary, describing an unpaid post

explanation.surface: A free drink, probably with a dash of soda water added.
explanation.walkthrough: An honorary secretary or treasurer works without pay, so 'not paid' points to the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A soda siphon is a pressurised bottle that dispenses fizzy water, so soda is often found in one.

clue.text: Guy, classy trainee, receiving article by hand

indicators.note: receiving means taking in, so the article goes inside the pair before it

blocks.note: a guy is a man
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U
the indefinite article
L is for learner, as on L-plates

explanation.surface: A smart young apprentice being handed some item in person.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from 1950s British talk of U and non-U speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Manual means done with the hands rather than by machine, from the Latin for hand.

clue.text: Wait for a sober man to finish

blocks.note: taken as written
TT stands for teetotal, a person who never drinks
the end is the finish

explanation.surface: Hang around until a man who doesn't drink has wrapped things up.
explanation.definitionFit: To attend on someone is to wait on or serve them, an older sense of wait for.

clue.text: Saw coloured salesman inside

indicators.note: inside says one part sits within the word for coloured

blocks.note: tan as an adjective: coloured a yellowish brown
a rep is a sales representative

explanation.surface: Someone spotted a tanned travelling salesman indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past tense of see; it is a noun, a surgical cutting tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A trepan is a cylindrical surgical saw used to cut a hole in the skull.

clue.text: A mind not maybe fitted for ruling

indicators.note: maybe signals one possible arrangement among many of the preceding letters

blocks.note: the letters of all three words

explanation.surface: A doubtful judgement that someone without much of a mind may still be suited to govern.
explanation.definitionFit: Being dominant means having power and control over others, the quality a ruler needs.

clue.text: Ideal state would put opiates on prescription

indicators.note: a prescription is dispensed in a measured portion, so a run of letters is taken from inside the phrase

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A society where opium-based drugs are freely prescribed would be some people's paradise.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas More's Utopia named an imaginary perfect society, and the word now means any ideal place.

clue.text: Pub where a parasite holds a man back

indicators.note: holds means the parasite grips the other part within it
back means going the reverse way, so that word runs from its end

blocks.note: a louse is a parasitic insect
he stands for a male person

explanation.surface: A grimy bar where a sponger keeps somebody pinned against the wall.
explanation.definitionFit: An ale-house is an old word for a pub or tavern, a house that serves ale.

clue.text: Do away with sound sort of vehicle

indicators.note: sound tells the solver to listen to the phrase rather than read it

blocks.note: to do away with is to kill

explanation.surface: Get rid of a decent kind of car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like an adjective meaning reliable; it is the cue to hear the word for kill.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleigh is a sledge drawn by horses or reindeer, a vehicle running on snow.

clue.text: Red, blind, new but spotted

indicators.note: new means made anew, so the letters before it are put in a fresh order

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: Someone colour-blind yet still manages to notice something.
explanation.definitionFit: A brindled coat is brownish with darker streaks or patches, so it is marked or spotted.
